lesson_title: Super Balls and Drum-Tight Bottles: the Gas Laws
hook_text: A capped bottle left in a hot car goes drum-tight by 3 pm — and nobody added a single molecule of air.
clip_script: A capped water bottle forgotten in a parked car on a blazing afternoon goes drum-tight by three o'clock. Nobody added air. The heat simply quickened the balls inside, and quicker balls knock harder. Here's the picture: a gas is a sealed room of super balls that never slow down — trillions of molecules caroming off the walls. Every hit is a tiny knock, and the endless drizzle of knocks is pressure. Now crush the bottle in your hand instead: same balls, smaller room, every ball reaches a wall more often — the drizzle thickens, and the bottle fights your grip. Half the volume, double the pressure. That's Boyle's law, and your bicycle pump preaches it on every stroke. And the finale: one equation, pV equals nRT, connects the drizzle, the room, the temperature — and the NUMBER of balls. Which means a pressure gauge, a measuring jug and a thermometer can count molecules you will never see. A census of the invisible, read off the noise on the walls. That's the whole topic.
visual_style: A car dashboard heat-shimmer shot of a swelling bottle; X-ray view revealing glowing ricocheting balls; a fist crushing a bottle as wall-ripples intensify; closing shot of gauge, jug and thermometer wiring into pV = nRT.
mood: Tactile and wonder-driven — physics felt in the palm, ending on a magic trick that is pure logic.
pacing: Hot-car mystery open, kinetic mid-section with the crush, slow satisfying equation reveal.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and turn both gas equations into one-line answers.
